newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Hopes for IMF support boost Tanzanian prospects.
newsitem.headline: Hopes for IMF support boost Tanzanian prospects.

text.p: News that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is likely to restore Tanzania's credit facilities -- suspended since 1992 -- has raised confidence in the prospects for economic revival.

But leading businessmen in the commercial capital, Dar es Salaam, warned that Tanzania, with an annual income of about $180 per head, still had far to go to emerge from the list of the world's poorest countries.

IMF's representative in Tanzania, Festus Osunsade, told Reuters in an interview that final talks were under way for an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) worth about $234 million to be approved by October.
The World Bank would then be ready to advance loans of $100 million and the Paris Club of Western donors was expected to approve debt relief amounting to $220 million.
Osunsade said the approval of the ESAF would lead to a resumption of donor aid now suspended.

The IMF has complained that Tanzania has been unable to balance its accounts, and has shown a lax attitude regarding tax collection. But a new Tanzania Revenue Authority had been a major factor in boosting government revenue, he said.
A bank official said: "Basically speaking, the government is getting its act together and adjusting to financial reality."
He said annual economic growth was now estimated at 5 percent while inflation, which peaked at 42 percent early last year, was down to 20 percent in July and falling.
In its August report, the Bank of Tanzania said the foreign trade account had improved, showing a deficit of $66.9 million for July against $94.2 million for the same period a year ago.
Exports in July were valued at $49.1 million, compared with $27.4 million in 1995, while imports dipped to $115.9 million against $121.6 million.
The Tanzanian shilling has remained stable, hovering between 590 and 596 to the U.S. dollar for the last three months, dealers said.

But economists warned that the country still had to overcome some of the legacy of the disastrous socialist economic policies introduced in 1967, involving widespread nationalisation and farm collectivisation.
Corruption, another problem, recently triggered warnings from Nordic governments who head the list of aid donors to Tanzania.
"We're talking about corruption which has come about by greed," Bo Garansson, director-general of the Swedish International Development Agency (SIDA) told Reuters on a visit to Tanzania.

The government recently announced a probe into allegations that senior ministers and officials received up to 900 million shillings in bribes in a conspiracy to avoid payment of import duties on a consignment of edible oil.

The IMF says it wants to see a speeding up of the programme to privatise parastatal organisations which have been supported by government subsidies. It has also urged a reduction in the number of government ministries.
Another problem is the volume of imports flowing into mainland Tanzania via Zanzibar -- where the semi-autonomous government levies lower import tariffs.
The IMF has urged a harmonisation of duties throughout the republic, which covers both Zanzibar and the mainland.
